newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Europe's currency pegs are stability anchor.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Europe's currency pegs are stability anchor.

text.p: Tough currency rules in the countries of eastern Europe should provide an anchor of stability during the difficult transition to a market economy, according to the experts who helped draft the plans.

The regimes, from Bulgaria's new and inflexible currency board, to the downward-drifting corridors favoured elsewhere in the region, are backed by the International Monetary Fund because they steer states towards the low inflation of Europe and the United States, where anchor currencies are from.

But domestic monetary policy can then only play a limited role and massive global capital flows mean there is always the risk of a Thai-style crunch -- when a country is forced to devalue its currency after speculators step in.
If the anchor slips, a country trying to hold it against the tide of the market loses credibility and the financial world is confronted with another currency storm.
But the IMF and other international experts believe the anti-inflation gains outweigh the problems from the speculators or the loss of a fully independent central bank.
DON'T HAUL THE CURRENCY ANCHOR YET

"I am reluctant to just tell countries...which use the exchange rate as an anchor to bring inflation down to give it up," IMF First Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer told a recent news briefing.

"The Czech Republic, Poland and others have gained in terms of stabilising their economies through having a peg. The Poles moved very rapidly to a crawling peg and next to a widening of the band. They moved very intelligently."

The IMF is bankrolling most of the countries seeking to make the transition from communism to capitalism with loans worth billions of dollars. But payments depend on a country meeting targets on spending, prices or monetary growth.

Several transition countries have had problems, but the overall trend is clear. Currencies are stabilizing, inflation and interest rates have mostly been coming down and -- in many countries -- growth is fairly strong.
"High inflation countries tend to have lower growth and a greater variability of output growth," said an IMF working paper published earlier this month.
"This deleterious effect on growth...is discernible at inflation rates above 10 percent per year and is particularly pronounced at inflation rates above 40 percent per year."
CREDIBLE CURRENCY PEG CAN BRING RAPID BENEFITS
Analysts say the experience of eastern Europe shows that the benefits of a currency peg can come very fast indeed, provided the peg is credible and coupled with restrictive monetary policies.

Bulgarian monthly inflation -- 243 percent in February alone -- is forecast to fall to around two percent for the rest of this year, partly due to the restrictions of the currency board introduced on July 1.

"The currency board is doing very well, better than we expected," said IMF Bulgaria mission chief Anne McGuirk. "Interest rates have come down to around six percent for short-term paper, money is flowing back into the system."

Other international monetary sources admitted that policies pegging one currency to another or to a basket of currencies carried certain risks, notably how to move away from the peg, or what to do if the markets turned vicious.
"The authorities cannot beat the market at the point when the market turns against a currency," said one source, who asked not to be identified.

"If the rate became unsustainable, maybe because of developments in the current account or the balance of payments...the cost of trying to maintain an exchange rate peg are such that it will have to go."
CURRENCY PEG MUST BE BACKED BY PROPER POLICIES
Fischer said the key thing was to act in time. "You should always move away from a peg before the crunch, the question is when you have a crunch," he said.

The Czech Republic was the most recent central European victim of the currency speculators and Prague allowed the crown to float in May after sharply higher interest rates failed to halt a currency decline.
"In the case of the Czech Republic, until very shortly before the markets turned against the currency, the pressure was for appreciation rather than for depreciation," the monetary source said.
"A country's tools are maintainance of policy that would satisfy markets that the rate is sustainable."

The experts saw little risk of Asia's currency turmoil spilling over into the European markets, noting that investors were able to discriminate between countries on the basis of their fundamentals and their readiness to look for IMF help.
Thai officials said on Monday they were looking at IMF backing to cope with their currency crisis.

The Philippines, forced to float the peso shortly after the Thai baht was floated, has won a promise of $1.1 billion in emergency funding to help ease the payments crunch, and some of the money has already been received.
